History:
• 32-yo female (Maria, DOB 22-Mar-1990) with sudden-onset left-sided headache beginning ~4 hours ago this morning.  
• Character: unilateral, sharp/severe, rated ~6/10 (kidney stone pain =10).  
• Associated symptoms: blurred vision with “zig-zag” lines, dizziness, photophobia (cannot tolerate screens), nausea, two episodes of vomiting at onset; worsens with head movement/standing; no limb weakness, no gait disturbance, no speech changes.  
• Tried paracetamol ~3 hours ago – no relief.  
• First episode of this type; no prior similar headaches.  
• Concerned about serious intracranial pathology (tumor, stroke).  
• Menstrual/pregnancy status: pregnancy considered “really doubt it.”  

Past Medical History:
• Remote kidney stone.  
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Family history: mother – migraine; hypothyroidism in family.  
• Medications: none.  
• Allergies: none known.  

Physical Examination:
(Limited to teleconsult/history)  
• Patient alert, oriented, conversant.  
• Appears distressed by pain, prefers head immobile.  
• No reported focal neurological deficits (no weakness, normal gait by history).  
• Vision: subjective blurring with visual aura‐type lines.  
• No reported throat swelling or other systemic findings.  

Impression:
• Probable migraine with aura.

Management Plan:
• Trial of ibuprofen (dose/route/frequency not documented) plus over-the-counter anti-sickness medication (name/dose not documented).  
• Encourage intake of sugary, carbonated drink (e.g., cola).  
• Arrange same-day in-person appointment for full neurological examination; patient may cancel if symptoms resolve.  
• Educated on expected course (may improve within 30–40 min of treatment; migraines can last 4–72 h).  
• Red-flag advice: seek urgent care/A&E if worsening pain, new neurological deficits, persistent vomiting, or other concerning changes.  

Patient Summary:
Maria developed a sudden unilateral left headache with aura, nausea, and vomiting—classic for migraine and without focal deficits. She will start analgesic and anti-emetic therapy now and attend an in-person review today unless symptoms fully settle.

Key Takeaways:
1. Take ibuprofen and an anti-sickness tablet as soon as possible; sip a sugary fizzy drink.  
2. If pain or visual disturbance has not improved in ~40 min, or if new symptoms such as weakness or confusion appear, go to A&E or call the practice urgently.  
3. Attend the arranged appointment today for examination, but cancel if completely recovered.

Next Steps:
• Obtain full neurological examination and vital signs at face-to-face visit.  
• Consider migraine-specific therapy (e.g., triptan) if inadequate response.  
• Follow-up call/visit if recurrent episodes; discuss preventive options if migraines become frequent.
